subsystems.name: Topological material
subsystems.role: where the exotic quantum states are supposed to live.
parts: epitaxial aluminium shell grown without breaking vacuum
or a two-dimensional hybrid with a superconducting layer

subsystems.name: Gate electrodes
subsystems.role: locally tune the electron density and create the conditions for Majorana modes.

subsystems.name: Device architecture
subsystems.role: arranges several nanowire segments so that pairs of modes can be created, moved and exchanged.
parts: tunnel junctions to normal-metal readout contacts

subsystems.name: Cryogenic and magnet system
subsystems.role: the physics only appears near absolute zero and in a magnetic field.

subsystems.name: Readout
subsystems.role: detects the parity of the modes, which is what carries the quantum information.

subsystems.name: Control and software layer
subsystems.role: sequences the voltages that create, braid and measure qubits.

buildSteps.title: Grow the hybrid material
buildSteps.detail: A semiconductor nanowire and a thin superconducting shell are grown together in a vacuum chamber so the interface stays atomically clean — dirty interfaces are the main reason signals have been ambiguous.

buildSteps.title: Pattern the device
buildSteps.detail: Electron-beam lithography defines gates, contacts and junctions on a substrate; the wires are placed or grown in position and connected by metal.

buildSteps.title: Tune into the topological regime
buildSteps.detail: A magnetic field is applied and gate voltages are adjusted until the wire is expected to host a pair of Majorana zero modes, one at each end.

buildSteps.title: Verify the modes
buildSteps.detail: Tunnelling spectroscopy looks for a zero-bias conductance peak. That peak alone is not proof, so the accepted test is a 'gap protocol': the energy gap must open and close in the pattern only the topological phase predicts.

buildSteps.title: Build a small qubit
buildSteps.detail: Four modes are arranged on one device; the way their parities pair up stores one qubit of information non-locally, so it is insensitive to local noise.

buildSteps.title: Measure parity
buildSteps.detail: A tunnel junction to a nearby sensor reads whether the paired modes hold an even or odd number of electrons.

buildSteps.title: Braiding
buildSteps.detail: Voltages are pulsed to physically move modes around one another. The order of the moves, not their speed, determines the operation — this is the fault tolerance. It has not been demonstrated.

buildSteps.title: Scale to an array
buildSteps.detail: Repeat the unit thousands of times with wiring and control that works at millikelvin temperatures.

prerequisites.why: majorana-like signals have appeared mainly in devices where disorder and unwanted states can mimic them.
the whole approach rests on their existence; the field is still arguing over evidence.
no experiment has shown that swapping the excitations performs the protected operation the theory requires.
dilution refrigerators are standard, but a useful machine needs thousands of wires inside one.
conventional room-temperature racks cannot wire up a large array without drowning it in heat and noise.

pathway.milestone: careful spectroscopy on nanowire hybrids, and a repeating argument about whether zero-bias peaks are real Majorana modes or disorder
pathway.unlocks: better materials, cleaner growth and stricter verification tests.

pathway.milestone: a device where braiding is demonstrated and the result is reproduced by an independent group
pathway.unlocks: confidence that the qubit concept works at all.

pathway.milestone: a single protected qubit that stays coherent far longer than conventional superconducting qubits
pathway.unlocks: a reason to engineer arrays rather than individual devices.

pathway.milestone: a few hundred to a few thousand logical-quality qubits with cryogenic control
pathway.unlocks: fault-tolerant machines for materials simulation and cryptanalysis — the prize that has driven the field since the 1990s.
